# Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Joint diseases > Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/6q0jzS)

---

## Summary

<u>Calcium</u> <u>pyrophosphate</u> deposition (CPPD) disease is a crystalline inflammatory <u>arthritis</u> seen primarily in individuals over age 60. It results from the deposition of <u>calcium</u> <u>pyrophosphate</u> dihydrate (<u>CPP</u>) crystals within <u>articular cartilage</u>. While it is typically <u>idiopathic</u>, it may also be caused by <u>joint</u> damage, various metabolic abnormalities, or a genetic predisposition. CPPD disease can be asymptomatic or manifest with acute or chronic symptoms. <u>Pseudogout</u> refers to <u>acute CPP crystal arthritis</u>, which typically presents as sporadic flares of monoarticular <u>synovitis</u> affecting a <u>large joint</u> and can last for much longer than a typical <u>gout flare</u>. <u>Chronic CPP crystal arthritis</u> has many clinical <u>phenotypes</u>, the most common of which resembles severe <u>osteoarthritis</u>. Identification of <u>CPP crystals</u> on <u>synovial fluid analysis</u> or on imaging in a patient with typical symptoms confirms the diagnosis. Treatment is primarily symptomatic and consists of antiinflammatory medications (including intraarticular and <u>systemic glucocorticoids</u>, <u>colchicine</u>, and <u>NSAIDs</u>). There is currently no specific treatment targeted at <u>CPP crystals</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♂</u> = <u>♀</u> [[1]](/library/J_bs6w)

* Age of onset: adults > 60 years [[1]](/library/J_bs6w)

* <u>Prevalence</u>: 8–10 million adults in the US  [[1]](/library/J_bs6w)[[2]](/library/EtX82-)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* The primary (<u>idiopathic</u>) form is most common, with age as a major <u>risk factor</u>. [[3]](/library/ouX0H-)

* Secondary forms [[3]](/library/ouX0H-)[[4]](/library/0fbekG)

* <u>Joint</u> trauma/damage: including <u>joint</u> <u>surgery</u>, previous <u>juvenile idiopathic arthritis</u>, and <u>osteoarthritis</u> [[1]](/library/J_bs6w)

* Metabolic disorders: including <u>hyperparathyroidism</u>, <u>hemochromatosis</u>,;  <u>hypomagnesemia</u>, <u>hypophosphatasia</u>, and possibly <u>gout</u>

* Familial <u>chondrocalcinosis</u>: due to mutations in the CCAL1 or CCAL2 <u>genes</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

Deposition of <u>calcium</u> <u>pyrophosphate</u> dihydrate (<u>CPP</u> or CPPD) crystals in <u>articular cartilage</u> → <u>paroxysmal</u> <u>joint</u> inflammation and <u>cartilage</u> destruction → inflammatory <u>arthritis</u> (<u>crystalline arthritis</u>)

---

## Clinical features

There are several distinct clinical <u>phenotypes</u> of CPPD disease. CPPD may also remain asymptomatic and be identified incidentally on imaging (asymptomatic <u>chondrocalcinosis</u>).  [[1]](/library/J_bs6w)[[2]](/library/EtX82-)[[4]](/library/0fbekG)




### Acute CPP crystal arthritis (<u>pseudogout</u>)




* Clinical features

* Acute attack of <u>pain</u> and swelling in the affected <u>joint</u>(s)

* <u>Monoarthritis</u> (occasionally <u>oligoarthritis</u>)

* Most commonly affects the knee and wrist; can also affect other <u>large joints</u> (e.g., hips, ankles)

* Typically <u>self-limited</u>

* Features that differ from <u>acute gout</u>

* Longer duration of acute attacks

* Possible systemic symptoms  [[5]](/library/sXXtz9)

* Triggers: can occur spontaneously or be triggered by <u>joint</u> trauma/<u>surgery</u> or acute illness  [[4]](/library/0fbekG)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Pseudogout</u> refers to the acute, not chronic, form of CPPD disease.




### Chronic CPP crystal arthritis




* <u>Osteoarthritis</u>-like presentation (<u>osteoarthritis</u> with CPPD; pseudo-<u>osteoarthritis</u>) ;  [[3]](/library/ouX0H-)

* Most common form of CPPD disease

* Characterized by progressive <u>joint</u> degeneration

* Usually polyarticular; can occur in <u>joints</u> not typically affected by OA

* More severe than typical OA

* Often associated with <u>pseudogout</u>-like flares of acute inflammatory <u>arthritis</u>

* <u>Rheumatoid arthritis</u>-like presentation (chronic <u>CPP crystal</u> inflammatory <u>arthritis</u>)

* Manifests similarly to <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u> (<u>RA</u>), with polyarticular distribution associated with morning stiffness

* In contrast to typical <u>RA</u>, <u>joint</u> involvement may be asymmetric and sequential.  [[4]](/library/0fbekG)

* Less common <u>phenotypes</u>

* Pseudoneuropathic <u>arthropathy</u>: manifests with destructive <u>monoarthritis</u> similar to <u>neuropathic arthropathy</u>, but sensation and <u>proprioception</u> are preserved [[6]](/library/M9XMLZ0)

* Crowned dens syndrome: <u>CPP</u> inflammatory <u>arthritis</u> of the C2 <u>vertebra</u>; causes acute <u>neck pain</u> resembling <u>meningitis</u> or <u>vertebral osteomyelitis</u> [[4]](/library/0fbekG)[[7]](/library/m9XVLZ0)

---

## Diagnosis

There are currently no validated diagnostic criteria for CPPD disease. Diagnosis is based on the identification of <u>CPP crystals</u> on <u>synovial fluid analysis</u> and/or the presence of <u>cartilage</u> calcification on imaging in a patient with suggestive symptoms.   [[2]](/library/EtX82-)[[6]](/library/M9XMLZ0)




### <u>Arthrocentesis</u> and <u>synovial fluid analysis</u> (<u>SFA</u>) [[4]](/library/0fbekG)




* The most accurate diagnostic method, but crystals can often be difficult to identify.  [[2]](/library/EtX82-)

* Expected findings

* <u>Polarized light microscopy</u> (with a red filter) appearance of CPP crystals 

* Rhomboid-shaped crystals that are weakly positively <u>birefringent</u>

* Crystals appear blue when their optical axis is oriented parallel to the polarizer.

* Crystals appear yellow when their axis is perpendicular to the polarizer.

* Cell count: <u>WBC</u> > 2,000/Î¼L with > 50% <u>neutrophils</u>  [[4]](/library/0fbekG)

* See also “<u>Interpretation of synovial fluid analysis</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> <u>SFA</u> can be <u>falsely negative</u>, as <u>CPPD crystals</u> are small and weakly <u>birefringent</u>. A negative <u>SFA</u> does not rule out CPPD disease. [[1]](/library/J_bs6w)[[6]](/library/M9XMLZ0)

### Imaging [[1]](/library/J_bs6w)[[4]](/library/0fbekG)[[8]](/library/K9XUoZ0)




* <u>X-ray</u> of the affected <u>joint</u>(s)

* Chondrocalcinosis: calcification of <u>cartilage</u> in the affected <u>joints</u>   [[2]](/library/EtX82-)

* Appears as radiodense shadows within the <u>cartilage</u>

* Types of <u>cartilage</u> involved:

* <u>Fibrocartilage</u> (<u>meniscus</u>, <u>annulus fibrosus</u> of intervertebral disk)

* Articular <u>hyaline cartilage</u>

* <u>Sensitivity</u>: ∼ 40% (i.e., <u>x-ray</u> may appear normal) [[8]](/library/K9XUoZ0)

* <u>Ultrasound</u> of the affected <u>joint</u>(s)

* <u>Hyperechoic</u> deposits within <u>cartilage</u>  [[1]](/library/J_bs6w)

* Operator-dependent; good <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u> if performed by experienced sonographers [[8]](/library/K9XUoZ0)

* Other modalities [[8]](/library/K9XUoZ0)

* CT: can be used to identify <u>chondrocalcinosis</u>; not typically used to evaluate <u>joint</u> <u>pain</u>

* <u>MRI</u>: not a sensitive/specific modality for diagnosing CPPD

* Dual-energy CT shows promise, but is not yet widely in use.

### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




* Serum <u>uric acid</u>

* Obtain in patients with <u>acute CPP crystal arthritis</u> to differentiate it from <u>gout</u>.

* Typically normal in CPPD

* Tests to rule out <u>differential diagnoses of inflammatory arthritis</u>: e.g., <u>CBC</u>, <u>rheumatoid factor</u>, <u>anti-CCP antibodies</u>

* Evaluate for underlying metabolic disorders if appropriate : e.g., obtain serum levels of <u>iron</u>, <u>transferrin</u>, <u>ferritin</u>, <u>calcium</u>, <u>magnesium</u>, <u>PTH</u>, and <u>alkaline phosphatase</u>  [[4]](/library/0fbekG)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* Other inflammatory arthritides, e.g.:

* <u>Gout</u> and other <u>crystalline arthropathies</u> (e.g., <u>basic calcium phosphate crystal deposition disease</u>)

* <u>Rheumatoid arthritis</u>

* <u>Seronegative spondyloarthropathies</u> (e.g., <u>psoriatic arthritis</u>, <u>reactive arthritis</u>)

* See also “<u>Differential diagnoses of inflammatory arthritis</u>.”

* <u>Septic arthritis</u> (in patients with <u>acute CPPD</u>): See “<u>Interpretation of synovial fluid analysis</u>.”

* <u>Osteoarthritis</u> and <u>erosive osteoarthritis</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

Management of CPPD is primarily symptomatic, as there is currently no therapy that can prevent or treat <u>CPP crystal</u> deposition in <u>cartilage</u>. [[1]](/library/J_bs6w)




* All patients: Treat any underlying condition (e.g., <u>hyperparathyroidism</u>, <u>hemochromatosis</u>).

* Asymptomatic patients: no further treatment required

* <u>Acute CPP crystal arthritis</u> (<u>pseudogout</u>): Symptomatic therapeutic options in order of preference include the following.  [[4]](/library/0fbekG)
1. * <u>Intraarticular injection</u> of <u>glucocorticoid</u>, with or without prior <u>joint aspiration</u> [[1]](/library/J_bs6w)
2. * <u>Colchicine</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE
3. * <u>NSAIDs</u>, e.g., <u>naproxen</u> DOSAGE (prescribe with a <u>proton pump inhibitor</u>)
4. * <u>Systemic glucocorticoids</u> (oral or parenteral), e.g., <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Chronic CPP crystal arthritis</u> [[4]](/library/0fbekG)

* Same antiinflammatory therapies as above

* Sometimes in combination

* Prophylaxis: Consider low-dose <u>colchicine</u> to decrease the frequency of acute attacks. [[4]](/library/0fbekG)
